name: Côte Atlantique
subtitle: Brittany & Normandy

days.title: Bremen → Crozon
days.detail: The long one, done while everyone is fresh. ~1 250 km of autobahn and autoroute. Two drivers, early start, pitch at dusk.

days.title: Crozon & Menez-Hom
days.detail: Camaret-sur-Mer, Pointe de Pen-Hir, Cap de la Chèvre — then out of the peninsula rather than doubling back: the Aulne estuary, Menez-Hom, Locronan, home along the Douarnenez bay.

days.title: Pointe du Raz & Cap Sizun
days.detail: South around the Baie de Douarnenez to the westernmost headland and the Baie des Trépassés, back along the full Cap Sizun coast road.

days.title: Crozon → Perros-Guirec
days.detail: Strike camp, ~160 km north across Finistère. Pitch by early afternoon, then ride the Ploumanac'h coast path road. Half a day of light is all you get.

days.title: Côte de Granit Rose & Trégor
days.detail: The pink granite stretch is only ~20 km, so build the day around it: Trégastel and Trébeurden, then the Trégor interior and the Jaudy and Trieux estuaries. Best surface of the trip.

days.title: Baie de Morlaix & Plougasnou
days.detail: East along the estuaries to Morlaix, out to the Plougasnou headland, home the long way over the Monts d'Arrée foothills.

days.title: Perros-Guirec → Saint-Malo
days.detail: ~140 km east along the north coast. Afternoon out to Cap Fréhel and Fort la Latte once the tent is up.

days.title: Mont-Saint-Michel & Côte d'Émeraude
days.detail: Down through Dol-de-Bretagne to the bay, up into the Cotentin edge at Granville, back along the Côte d'Émeraude. Go early — the causeway fills by ten.

days.title: Saint-Malo → Bayeux
days.detail: ~180 km into Normandy. Afternoon shakeout along the Côte de Nacre once camp is set.

days.title: D-Day beaches & Cotentin
days.detail: Omaha and Utah, Pointe du Hoc, then as far up the Cotentin as the light allows. Last full day — keep fuel in hand.

days.title: Bayeux → Bremen
days.detail: ~900 km home. Shorter than the way out, which is the whole point of running the route east.

campsiteCaveat: Coastal campsites in Brittany and Normandy close between 15 and 30 September — the Bayeux end of Plan A sits inside that window. Provence runs later, but the mountain sites at Sospel and Castellane close earlier than the coast. No closing date here has been confirmed. These need phone calls, not more reading.

items.title: Four reflective stickers per helmet
items.why: Front, back and both sides, at least 18 cm² each. Without them a helmet counts as unapproved in France — €135. Applies to foreign riders too.

items.title: CE-approved gloves, rider and pillion
items.why: Mandatory since 2016. Ordinary gloves do not count — look for the CE / EN 13594 mark.

items.title: Hi-vis vest per rider, reachable from the saddle
items.why: The law says within reach while seated, so tank bag or under the seat — not buried in a pannier. Fine rises sharply if you are stopped at the roadside without it.

items.title: Dipped headlight on at all times
items.why: Required day and night for motorcycles.

items.title: Crit’Air sticker — check your route
items.why: Low-emission zones cover Rennes and Rouen among others, and rules have been in flux. Order online well ahead if the van route touches a city; the sticker is a few euros and takes days to arrive.

items.title: Insurance certificate for each bike
items.why: A green card is no longer needed between EU countries, but carry your Versicherungsbestätigung anyway — it settles roadside questions fast.

items.title: Insurance for the bikes while inside the transporter
items.why: The gap people miss. Many motor policies do not cover a bike being carried as cargo. Confirm with your insurer in writing before you load.

items.title: Zulassungsbescheinigung Teil I for every vehicle
items.why: Bikes and the transporter.

items.title: Driving licences and ID or passports
EHIC / European health card
items.why: On the back of your German Krankenkasse card.

items.title: Breakdown cover valid in France, including bike recovery
items.why: Check the policy covers a motorcycle and, separately, the transporter.

items.title: Written permission if you ride a bike registered to someone else
Ratchet straps and soft loops
items.why: Four points per bike. Soft loops save your bars and fork tubes.

items.title: Front wheel chock or a proper front strap setup
Check total weight and axle load with bikes aboard
Somewhere secure to leave the empty van at each campsite
items.why: Ask when booking — some sites charge for a second vehicle or cap length.

items.title: Tyres with real tread left
items.why: Atlantic September means wet granite and wet paint lines. This is the one to not economise on.

items.title: Puncture repair kit and a mini compressor
Basic tools and a spare clutch or brake lever
Chain lube
items.why: Coastal salt air and rain will strip it inside a week.

items.title: Rain gear you actually trust
items.why: Expect at least one properly wet day in Finistère.

items.title: Warm layer
items.why: Coastal wind makes 16 °C feel a lot colder at speed.

items.title: Clear visor or spare
items.why: A dark visor is useless in Breton drizzle at 19:30.

items.title: Tent that handles wind, plus solid pegs
items.why: Coastal pitches are exposed and often sandy. Bring longer pegs than you think.

items.title: Campsite closing dates confirmed
items.why: Many coastal sites shut between 15 and 30 September — the Bayeux end of the trip sits in that window.

items.title: Camping gas — buy in France
items.why: Cartridges cannot travel in the van legally in any quantity. Pick up locally.

items.title: Cash and a second bank card
items.why: Rural French pumps are card-only after hours and sometimes reject foreign cards. Do not let the tank get low on a Sunday evening.

items.title: Offline maps downloaded
items.why: Signal is patchy on the Finistère headlands and in the Monts d’Arrée.

items.title: Tide times for the Mont-Saint-Michel day
Emergency number 112, and a contact left at home
